questions.stem:
Statements:
Only a few gadget are good
Some manual are memory
No memory is gadget
Conclusions:
I. All good being manual is a possibility
II. No gadget is manual
In the question below, some statements are given followed by two conclusions numbered I and II. You
have to take the given statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known
facts. Read all the conclusions and then decide which of the given conclusions logically follows from the
given statements, disregarding commonly known facts. Give answer -
options: If either conclusion I or II follows
If neither conclusion I nor II follows
If both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (a) If only conclusion I follows

Nothing prevents all good objects from also being manual; manual objects need not all be memory. Thus I is possible. Gadget–manual overlap is not determined, so the universal separation in II does not follow.

questions.stem:
Statements:
Only stadium are arena
Some match are stadium
All match are sport
Conclusions:
I. No arena being sport is a possibility
II. Some arena are not match
In the question below, some statements are given followed by two conclusions numbered I and II. You
have to take the given statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known
facts. Read all the conclusions and then decide which of the given conclusions logically follows from the
given statements, disregarding commonly known facts. Give answer -
options: If either conclusion I or II follows
If neither conclusion I nor II follows
If both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (b) If only conclusion II follows

"Only stadium are arena" ordinarily gives arena ⊆ stadium. It does not force an arena outside match, and it permits arena and sport to be disjoint. Thus the PDF's choice of only II is not justified by ordinary subset logic. Additional intended meaning of "only" is needed.

In the question below, some statements are given followed by two conclusions numbered I and II. You
have to take the given statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known

If both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (e) If both conclusions I and II follow

Some cities are markets and all markets are trade, so some cities are trade (I). Some trade being outside urban does not prevent every urban object from lying within trade. II is therefore possible as well.

In the question below, some statements are given followed by two conclusions numbered I and II. You

The floors–garden overlap is not fixed. "All floors are garden" and "Some floors are not garden" are complementary: either all floors lie in garden or at least one does not. The correct choice is either I or II.

questions.stem:
How is E related to F?
Study the information carefully and answer the questions given below.
In a family of eight members. A is the father of B. C is the daughter of F. G is the brother of H. B is the
sister - in - law of F. H has two daughters. B is not married. D has two children. E is the male member of
the family.
questions.explanation:
Source answer: (c) Son

The family arrangement used by the source is: A and H are the parents of B and D; G is H's brother; D and F are the parents of C and E. B is unmarried, so her sister D is married to F, making B F's sister-in-law. C is female and E is male, so E is F's son. H, B, D and C are the four females. If S marries G, S is H's sister-in-law.

who joined.
questions.explanation:

The new average is 15y/16. Thus (12y + 72)/14 = 15y/16, giving y = 64. The heavier new student weighs 40 kg and the other weighs 32 kg; the difference is 8 kg.

questions.explanation:

C = (100/9)% of A = A/9. Put A = 9k and B = 7k, so C = k. The total age is 3 × (22 + 8/12) = 68 years. Hence 17k = 68 and C is 4 years old.
